paragraphs: Sleep-stage classification often combines several kinds of physiological measurements. Combining them becomes difficult when different modalities disagree, especially because methods commonly assume that their information is well aligned. ConfSleepNet addresses this problem by making disagreement an explicit part of how it forms a prediction, rather than relying on alignment that may not hold in practice.

The framework first learns evidence for individual sleep stages from each modality. It uses different category structures to reflect differences between modalities, allowing their evidence to be organized in ways suited to their characteristics. Each view then produces an opinion containing both its prediction and its uncertainty. A conflict-aware aggregation mechanism combines these opinions into a joint decision.

The authors support the approach through theoretical analysis and experiments on sleep staging. The contribution is a way to carry uncertainty and disagreement through the combination process: the final decision depends on how the views support or conflict with one another. The reported findings support the effectiveness of this design for the studied sleep-staging tasks.
icml-2026-a-conflict-aware-evidential-fr.tldr: ConfSleepNet combines modality-specific evidence and uncertainty to resolve conflicting predictions in sleep-stage classification.

paragraphs: Distributed learning can spend substantial resources communicating gradient information between agents. Compressing that information reduces communication, but it can weaken the guarantees that optimization will converge. Error feedback offers a computationally inexpensive way to address this damage. With many versions available, however, understanding the relative performance of different error-feedback algorithms has remained difficult.

This paper develops tight convergence analyses for two established methods: classic Error Feedback, or EF, and Error Feedback 21, or EF21. The analysis identifies optimal step sizes and constructs a tailored Lyapunov function for each algorithm. These functions provide a mathematical way to track progress during optimization, making the choice of analytical tool part of obtaining sharp guarantees.

The resulting guarantees hold independently of how many agents participate and recover the best known guarantees in the single-agent setting. This connects the distributed analysis to an established reference case. The contribution is stronger theoretical understanding of these two methods and their tuning, helping clarify their behavior without introducing another error-feedback variant.
icml-2026-a-tight-theory-of-error-feedba.tldr: Tight analyses of EF and EF21 identify optimal step sizes and recover the best known single-agent convergence guarantees.

paragraphs: Low-rank compression reduces the computational demands of language models by approximating their weight matrices with smaller representations. Its success depends on two decisions: how much capacity to retain in each layer, and how to construct each approximation. This paper addresses both, arguing that existing error estimates miss propagation across layers and that some Fisher-based decompositions suffer severe rank collapse.

Layer-wise Error Modeling Search, or LEMS, estimates compression error using local layer importance, global importance, and a propagation bias. It then allocates ranks across the model through an integer linear programming formulation. The accompanying KFAC-SVD method changes the decomposition itself, using token-level statistics to mitigate the rank deficiency found in earlier Fisher-based approaches.

Across Mistral, Qwen3, and Llama3 families, LEMS outperforms the tested search strategies, with zero-shot accuracy gains reaching 4.8 percentage points and results extending to 70-billion-parameter models. KFAC-SVD delivers an average perplexity improvement of 15%. These findings show benefits from improving both the allocation of compressed capacity and the quality of the retained representation.
icml-2026-advancing-svd-based-llm-compre.tldr: LEMS and KFAC-SVD improve language-model compression by refining layer-wise rank allocation and low-rank decomposition quality.

paragraphs: Training text contains descriptions of how AI systems behave, including accounts of both aligned and misaligned behavior. This paper asks whether those descriptions influence the behavior a model later exhibits. Its central hypothesis is that discourse about AI can establish behavioral expectations during pretraining, potentially making descriptions of misalignment partly self-fulfilling.

The authors test this hypothesis through controlled pretraining of 6.9-billion-parameter language models with different amounts of alignment-related discourse. Increasing the frequency of synthetic documents about AI misalignment raises measured misaligned behavior. Increasing documents about aligned behavior has the opposite effect, reducing misalignment scores from 45% to 9% in the reported comparison.

Post-training weakens these effects but does not eliminate them. The findings therefore support treating pretraining data as a contributor to alignment, alongside later interventions. The controlled changes provide evidence that AI discourse can shape downstream behavior in the studied setting. The authors call this area alignment pretraining and recommend considering alignment goals when constructing pretraining data, as well as when post-training models.
icml-2026-alignment-pretraining-ai-disco.tldr: Controlled pretraining experiments show that descriptions of aligned or misaligned AI behavior can shift models’ subsequent alignment.

paragraphs: Changing long passages of knowledge inside a language model requires keeping the resulting generation coherent. Earlier autoregressive editing methods can handle length more effectively, but their fixed-size chunks may cut across logical structure. AnyEdit++ addresses this issue by choosing editing segments according to the content, so that the boundaries reflect semantic changes within the material.

Its Bayes-Chunk mechanism uses Bayesian Surprise to identify those boundaries dynamically. The accompanying theory connects segmentation to two properties. First, cross-segment interference is minimized when anchor keys are geometrically orthogonal; the authors state that their surprise-based boundaries naturally satisfy this condition. Second, their analysis finds that applying updates at semantic peaks provides strictly better control than using arbitrary split points.

Experiments cover mathematical reasoning, code generation, and narrative tasks, with reported improvements in performance and robustness over state-of-the-art baselines. The results connect a practical editing choice to a structural explanation: where a passage is divided affects how independently and effectively its parts can be updated. The theoretical interference claim specifically rests on the stated geometric condition.
icml-2026-anyedit-adaptive-long-form-kno.tldr: AnyEdit++ uses Bayesian Surprise to choose semantic editing boundaries, improving long-form knowledge editing in the reported tasks.

paragraphs: A language-model benchmark score reflects more than the model being tested. Datasets, prompts, decoding choices, and the software and hardware used for evaluation all contribute to the outcome. This paper argues that attributing a score directly to intrinsic capability can therefore be misleading. It reports that evaluation choices alone can produce accuracy swings of up to 70%.

The proposed framework, LLM evaluatology, treats evaluation as a system whose components and interactions should be studied explicitly. Structured causal modeling supplies a way to reason about interventions. Factorial experimental design separates individual component effects from interaction effects, while interventions on individual questions probe how dataset construction influences measured performance.

This matters because evaluation questions vary across languages, domains, and usage styles, making a static benchmark an incomplete basis for attributing capability. By examining evaluation settings together with structured question variations, the framework aims to make results more interpretable and reproducible. Its contribution is a method for more careful attribution, including identifying circumstances in which strong scores may reflect dataset-related effects.
icml-2026-beyond-benchmarks-toward-causa.tldr: LLM evaluatology uses causal modeling and experimental design to separate model capability from effects of the evaluation setup.

paragraphs: A model that ranks labels can be confident about several different things: a complete ordering, the ordering of a subset, or which labels appear near the top. Calibration asks whether those probabilities agree with observed frequencies. This paper formalizes calibration for probabilistic label ranking, where treating every possible ranking as an ordinary class misses these different uses of predictions.

The authors establish a hierarchy covering full rankings, sub-rankings, and top-k rankings. Full-ranking calibration implies the other forms, but the reverse implications do not hold. Sub-ranking and top-k calibration are also incomparable: satisfying either one does not establish the other. Consequently, checking one ranking-related probability can leave a different aspect of reliability unresolved.

Experiments find that popular ranking models are often poorly calibrated and can behave quite differently under sub-ranking and top-k metrics. For RLHF reward models, calibration correlates strongly, but imperfectly, with benchmark accuracy. That relationship suggests calibration measures a useful quality dimension beyond getting the top choice right, motivating further work on its downstream effects and correction.
icml-2026-calibrated-preference-learning.tldr: The paper formalizes several distinct forms of ranking calibration and shows that accuracy alone does not fully capture them.

paragraphs: Working code can still contain duplication, unnecessary complexity, and architectural debt. Refactoring improves its structure while preserving behavior. CodeTaste examines two separate abilities of coding agents: carrying out a specified refactoring and recognizing the structural changes that human developers chose when given a broader area to improve.

The benchmark is built from large refactorings spanning multiple files in open-source repositories. Its scoring combines repository tests with tailored static checks. Tests assess whether behavior remains correct, while checks using dataflow reasoning verify that unwanted code patterns disappear and intended patterns appear. This allows evaluation to consider structural change alongside whether the resulting program still works.

The reported results reveal a gap between execution and discovery. Agents perform well with detailed refactoring instructions but often miss human choices when only given a focus area. Separating proposal generation from implementation improves alignment, and selecting the best-aligned proposal can improve it further. CodeTaste therefore provides both an evaluation target and a possible preference signal for teaching agents to make refactoring decisions closer to those of developers.
icml-2026-codetaste-can-llms-generate-hu.tldr: CodeTaste finds that coding agents implement specified refactorings more reliably than they discover the changes human developers chose.

paragraphs: Two independently trained neural networks may occupy different locations in parameter space while both achieving low loss. Mode connectivity asks whether a continuous path can join those solutions without passing through high-loss regions. Earlier empirical work has demonstrated such paths, but existing methods do not reliably connect every tested pair and have focused mainly on a limited collection of architectures.

This paper proposes an empirical algorithm for connecting independently trained solutions through layer-wise connectivity. Its evaluation expands the architectural scope to MobileNet, ShuffleNet, EfficientNet, RegNet, Deep Layer Aggregation, and Compact Convolutional Transformers. This broader coverage addresses whether connectivity methods remain useful beyond the basic convolutional networks and architectures emphasized in earlier studies.

The authors report more consistent connectivity paths across independently trained pairs, as well as support for models trained using different hyperparameters. These findings broaden the empirical evidence for constructing low-loss connections across network families and training choices. The contribution concerns the reliability and applicability of a practical connectivity algorithm; the stated results are empirical.
icml-2026-connecting-independently-train.tldr: A layer-wise connectivity algorithm constructs more consistent low-loss paths across independently trained models from a broader range of architectures.

paragraphs: Coupled cluster theory can predict molecular properties with accuracy beyond that commonly obtained from density functional theory, but its computational cost restricts its use. This paper introduces Molecular Orbital Learning, or MoLe, as a way to learn mathematical quantities used within coupled cluster calculations. The goal is to support accurate wavefunction-based modeling with machine learning.

MoLe is an equivariant model that takes mean-field Hartree-Fock molecular orbitals as input and directly predicts coupled cluster excitation amplitudes. These amplitudes are core objects of the coupled cluster method. Predicting them connects the learned model to the structure of the underlying calculation, rather than only producing a final molecular property.

The authors report strong data efficiency and generalization to larger molecules and geometries displaced from equilibrium, despite training only on small molecules at equilibrium. They also investigate whether MoLe can reduce the cycles needed for coupled cluster convergence. The findings position it as a possible foundation for accelerating molecular design with accurate wavefunction models and complementing force-field approaches.
icml-2026-coupled-cluster-con-mole-molec.tldr: MoLe predicts coupled cluster excitation amplitudes from molecular orbitals and shows strong generalization beyond its small-molecule training geometries.

paragraphs: Designing incentives means choosing interaction rules that lead multiple participants toward desirable equilibrium outcomes. Automating this process is difficult because equilibria can be computationally hard to obtain, non-unique, and unstable. Deep Incentive Design addresses the problem with a differentiable framework that incorporates equilibrium computation into the architecture used to learn incentive choices.

Its central modules are differentiable equilibrium blocks, or DEBs, designed to be game-agnostic. These blocks allow the framework to connect design decisions with the equilibria they produce during training. The authors use a unified pipeline to study three different tasks: contract design, machine scheduling, and inverse equilibrium problems. Each task uses a single trained neural network.

The architecture handles the full context-parameterized distribution of problem instances considered for each task, covering games with between two and sixteen actions per player. This makes the reported scope broader than solving one fixed interaction at a time. The findings support the use of a shared differentiable approach across these diverse incentive-design settings and game sizes.
icml-2026-deep-incentive-design-with-dif.tldr: Deep Incentive Design embeds differentiable equilibrium modules in a unified learning pipeline for several incentive-design tasks.

paragraphs: This study compares supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning for PlasmidGPT, a model that generates whole plasmid sequences. The reinforcement-learning approach uses GRPO with a reward based on functional annotations, length constraints, and repeat penalties. The study examines both whether generated sequences pass quality control and how post-training changes their broader statistical properties.

Across 4,000 sequences generated from eight prompts, the reinforcement-learning model achieves a 71.6% quality-control pass rate, compared with 4.3% for the pretrained model and 11.0% for supervised fine-tuning. A five-model reward ablation identifies the bonus for correct promoter-to-coding-sequence-to-terminator arrangement as critical. Rejection-sampling comparisons indicate that sampling more heavily from the original model does not recover the improvement.

The reinforcement-learning outputs also move toward real-plasmid distributions in three-base composition and minimum free energy density, although neither is directly rewarded. Energy density converges toward the real-plasmid regime under supervised fine-tuning as well. On a small curated hold-out set, reinforcement learning improves continuation log-likelihood for all 29 sequences, with a mean increase of 0.83 nats.
icml-2026-effects-of-structural-reward-s.tldr: Structural reward shaping substantially improves plasmid-generation quality control and shifts some unrewarded properties toward real-plasmid distributions.

paragraphs: Feature distillation trains a smaller vision transformer to reproduce a larger model’s internal representations. It often works between similarly sized models but struggles when the student is much narrower. This paper investigates an apparent contradiction: representations for each individual image are highly compressible, yet a narrow student with a linear projector still has difficulty matching the teacher.

The analysis finds that the low-rank subspace changes substantially across images. It also introduces Spectral Energy Patterns, revealing that tokens distribute energy broadly across channel modes even within low-rank subspaces. Together, these observations explain an encoding mismatch: compressibility for one image does not mean a fixed narrow representation can easily accommodate the teacher across the dataset.

Two small architectural changes address this mismatch. Lift keeps a lightweight widening projector during inference, while WideLast widens only the student’s final block. On ImageNet-1K, they raise DeiT-Tiny accuracy when distilled from CaiT-S24 from 74.86% to 77.53% and 78.23%, respectively. They also improve students trained without distillation, supporting the usefulness of additional representational bandwidth.
icml-2026-from-per-image-low-rank-to-enc.tldr: An encoding mismatch helps explain failed vision-transformer feature distillation, and two targeted widening changes improve compression results.

paragraphs: Data selection aims to retain a useful subset of training examples. One approach assigns each example a Data Shapley value or a related semivalue, then selects the highest-scoring examples. These values account for interactions across subsets, but earlier work has found cases where the resulting selection performs no better than random. This paper investigates how to use such information more effectively.

The proposed NASH framework decomposes the target utility, such as validation accuracy, into simpler component functions that are informative for Shapley-based selection. It then optimizes an objective that combines those components nonlinearly. The approach changes both the level at which usefulness is analyzed and how the resulting signals are assembled into a selection objective.

The authors report substantial improvements in the effectiveness of Shapley- and semivalue-based selection with minimal additional runtime. The finding supports a more structured use of data valuations: useful component-level information can contribute to better subset choices through nonlinear aggregation. It does not require interpreting the original top-scoring-example strategy as consistently effective across all settings.
icml-2026-is-data-shapley-not-better-tha.tldr: NASH improves Shapley-based data selection by decomposing utility into informative components and combining them nonlinearly.

paragraphs: Sparse Bayesian Learning identifies which features matter in a linear model through automatic relevance determination, or ARD. It encourages a compact model by optimizing the marginal likelihood. However, its usual assumption of equal noise variance across observations can make it sensitive to outliers or incorrectly specified noise, damaging both model fit and prediction.

This paper extends relevance learning to individual samples as well as individual features. A single Bayesian objective therefore determines which parts of the model and which observations should retain influence. This symmetric treatment enables simultaneous model and data sparsification, bringing the handling of contaminated observations into the same framework that selects useful features.

The extension preserves conjugacy and allows closed-form updates within standard optimization procedures, keeping the proposed approach mathematically tractable. The authors also connect it to robust regression and influence-function perspectives. Experiments across diverse regression tasks report models that are both sparse and robust. The findings support jointly learning feature and sample relevance when a feature-selection method alone is vulnerable to contaminated data.
icml-2026-joint-model-and-data-sparsific.tldr: Joint ARD learns feature and sample relevance together, producing sparse regression models that are more robust to contaminated data.

paragraphs: Detecting anomalies in a changing graph is difficult when few abnormal examples have labels. Unsupervised methods can produce unclear decision boundaries, while methods trained on a small labeled anomaly set can overfit those examples. This paper seeks a boundary learned from normal or unlabeled data that can also use anomaly labels when available without sacrificing generalization to unseen anomalies.

The framework has three components. Residual representations capture how current interactions differ from their historical context. A restriction loss places normal representations between two hyperspheres sharing the same center, maintaining consistent scales while keeping anomalies separable. A bi-boundary optimization strategy then uses the log-likelihood distribution modeled by a normalizing flow to learn a robust decision boundary.

The authors describe the framework as model-agnostic and report superior performance across diverse evaluation settings. Its design links temporal deviations, controlled representation geometry, and likelihood-based boundary learning. This combination addresses the tension between distinguishing known abnormal behavior and remaining sensitive to forms of anomaly that were not represented in the limited labeled examples.
icml-2026-learning-discriminative-and-ge.tldr: A model-agnostic framework combines temporal residuals and likelihood-based boundaries to detect dynamic-graph anomalies with limited supervision.

paragraphs: Federated learning becomes harder when participating clients have incorrect labels. The problem is compounded when clients differ in their data distributions, the kinds of label errors they contain, and how frequently those errors occur. This paper studies how information already present in the federated learning process can help correct labels and stabilize local training.

The motivating observation is that the global model memorizes noisy labels slowly. The authors interpret this as an opportunity: its predictions and representations can remain useful while local training faces corrupted supervision. Their Federated Global Reviser, or FedGR, uses this property through three cooperating modules that revise noisy labels and regularize client training in a self-contained method.

Across three widely used federated label-noise benchmarks, FedGR consistently outperforms eight state-of-the-art baselines, including under severe noise and data heterogeneity. These results support using the global model as a source of corrective information for local learning. The approach builds on the observed difference in noisy-label memorization, turning that behavior into a practical mechanism for greater robustness.
icml-2026-learning-locally-revising-glob.tldr: FedGR uses the global model’s slow memorization of noisy labels to revise supervision and improve federated-learning robustness.

paragraphs: Neural rough differential equations summarize finely sampled inputs so that hidden states can advance in larger integration steps, retaining accuracy under irregular sampling. Their usual mathematical structure follows Stratonovich calculus. This creates a limitation for Itô dynamics, which require quadratic-variation terms, and for manifold-valued Itô flows, where the ordering of covariant derivatives matters.

Branched Neural Rough Differential Equations replace this single algebraic setup with structures matched to the governing calculus. Rooted trees represent Euclidean Itô dynamics, planar rooted trees support ordered derivatives on manifolds, and the classical shuffle algebra remains available for Stratonovich dynamics. The framework treats coarse integration steps geometrically and exactly preserves the manifold constraints of its intrinsic dynamics.

The paper also introduces a branched signature-kernel training objective that exposes quadratic-variation terms, enabling Itô-consistent matching of probability laws. Applications include rough Bergomi volatility, simulation-to-real rotation forecasting on SO(3), and positive-definite covariance dynamics. Together, these results support a unified approach to learning stochastic and geometrically constrained dynamics beyond the usual Euclidean–Stratonovich setting.
icml-2026-learning-manifold-and-ito-dyna.tldr: B-NRDEs adapt rough differential equation models to Itô calculus and manifold geometry while preserving manifold constraints.

paragraphs: Correctly predicting a program’s output may reflect familiarity with conventional operators rather than careful use of supplied execution rules. PLSemanticsBench separates these possibilities by pairing small C programs with explicit formal semantics. It changes the meanings of familiar operators and introduces unfamiliar symbols whose meanings are available only through the supplied rules.

The benchmark probes rule composition for final states, rule selection when state remains unchanged, sustained conditioning over long traces, and behavior under novel semantics. It uses two semantic systems and three program sources: human-written, model-translated, and fuzzer-generated. Increasing structural complexity further tests whether models can continue following the rules as the programs become harder.

Across 11 frontier language models, final-state accuracy reaches up to 90% under standard semantics but drops by as much as 40–60 percentage points under semantic changes and greater complexity. Only a few models achieve nonzero long-horizon conditioning accuracy, with the best reaching 35%. These results suggest that tested models often rely on pretrained symbol associations instead of consistently applying the provided formal rules.
icml-2026-llms-lean-on-priors-not-progra.tldr: PLSemanticsBench finds sharp performance drops when program rules conflict with familiar symbol meanings or require sustained rule-following.

paragraphs: Language models can interpret meaning flexibly but make mistakes in complex logical reasoning. Formal solvers provide rigorous derivations, yet small syntax errors in a translated logic program can prevent them from helping. LogicSAGE combines these capabilities in a dual-process framework, pairing a neural reasoner with a symbolic validator.

Its central mechanism is Socratic Error Correction. Feedback from the solver becomes a signal for another round of reasoning and revision. Through this iterative exchange, the framework refines logic programs and resolves ambiguities in their meaning. The design therefore makes error correction part of the interaction between the neural and symbolic components, rather than treating solver feedback as the endpoint of an unsuccessful attempt.

Across five benchmarks, the reported 8-billion-parameter system achieves a state-of-the-art average accuracy of 92.36% and substantially outperforms the GPT-4 baselines studied. These results support the claim that architecture can outweigh model scale in faithful reasoning within the evaluated comparisons. The contribution is an integrated reasoning-and-validation process that uses feedback to improve the formal representation.
icml-2026-logicsage-neuro-symbolic-reaso.tldr: LogicSAGE iteratively uses symbolic-solver feedback to improve neural reasoning, achieving strong results with an 8-billion-parameter model.

paragraphs: Two-sample testing asks whether two collections of observations come from the same distribution. Methods that learn how to compare the collections often split data between learning and testing to control false positives. That division is awkward when reference data are abundant but only a handful of query observations are available. LOTTERY uses the imbalance as an opportunity.

The method learns representations using reference samples alone. Different representation families capture global and local structure of the reference distribution, providing signals for detecting departures from it. An uncertainty-guided principle assigns adaptive weights to these representations, also using only reference data. This places the representation-learning work on the abundant side of the comparison.

The theory establishes permutation-based type I error control and a conditional consistency result: as sample sizes grow, power approaches one if the representation collection includes at least one consistent representation. Experiments report strong performance across benchmarks while retaining false-positive control. The condition matters because the aggregation guarantee depends on having a representation capable of consistently detecting the departure.
icml-2026-lottery-learning-from-referenc.tldr: LOTTERY learns and weights representations from abundant reference data to support two-sample testing with very few query samples.

paragraphs: Adapting a vision–language model can create a trade-off between recognizing known classes and recognizing unseen ones. This paper examines a source of error beyond overfitting: asymmetric confusion, where one class is frequently mistaken for another but the reverse rarely happens. Such pretraining-induced preferences can persist for unseen classes even when tuning reduces them for known classes.

Neutral-Reference Prompting, or NeRP, corrects predictions without changing model parameters. It uses neutral text prompts and reference images to estimate class preferences along the model’s existing inter-class geometry. These preferences are combined with sample likelihood into a surrogate score. A local prediction flip is applied between confusable classes when the prior strongly favors the current answer but observed evidence is clearly insufficient.

Across multiple backbones and 15 few-shot and cross-domain benchmarks, NeRP substantially improves unseen-class accuracy while preserving known-class prediction performance. The findings support selectively correcting predictions dominated by prior preferences. The conditional flip mechanism is central: the method changes a prediction when its evidence and prior support meet the stated criteria.
icml-2026-neutral-reference-prompting-fo.tldr: NeRP corrects prior-dominated vision–language predictions, improving unseen-class recognition while preserving known-class performance in the reported benchmarks.

paragraphs: Deep Koopman modeling learns observable functions that allow nonlinear systems to be represented through a global linear model. Neural networks can learn these functions, but training both the representation and the dynamics effectively is difficult. Existing training approaches can create high optimization complexity or obstruct end-to-end learning, limiting accuracy and efficiency.

QPKO makes the linear model the output of a quadratic programming problem conditioned on the learned observables. Its objective emphasizes one-step prediction accuracy, while its constraints address accuracy over multiple steps. Because this optimization maps observable functions to the linear model, the latter no longer needs to be maintained as an independently trainable component.

The mapping is implemented with OptNet as a differentiable and computationally efficient module, allowing end-to-end training through the quadratic program. Experiments on four nonlinear dynamical systems report improvements in modeling accuracy, training efficiency, and control performance. The approach therefore links simpler outer optimization with a structured inner problem that explicitly considers both immediate and multi-step prediction behavior.
icml-2026-qpko-differentiable-qp-embedde.tldr: QPKO embeds a differentiable quadratic program in deep Koopman modeling to improve training efficiency, prediction, and control.

paragraphs: Conversational agents need to maintain useful knowledge about a user across sessions, even as preferences evolve and conversations contain conflicting evidence. Finite context windows and static model memory make this difficult. RGMem addresses the additional challenge of moving beyond individual remembered facts to infer more stable preferences and deeper user traits.

Inspired by the renormalization-group perspective on multiple scales, the framework turns conversational episodes into semantic facts and user insights. It progressively integrates them into a changing user profile through hierarchical coarse-graining, thresholded updates, and rescaling. The design explicitly distinguishes rapidly changing evidence from slowly varying traits and allows nonlinear, phase-transition-like changes in the profile.

Experiments on LOCOMO and PersonaMem report consistent improvements over state-of-the-art memory systems, including stronger continuity across sessions and better adaptation to evolving preferences. These results support organizing memory at several levels of abstraction rather than relying solely on fact retrieval or static summaries. The contribution is a process for continuously updating a user model while treating short-term evidence and longer-term characteristics differently.
icml-2026-rgmem-renormalization-groupins.tldr: RGMem transforms conversational episodes into evolving, multi-level user profiles to improve continuity and personalization across sessions.

paragraphs: Using language models to judge generated outputs raises a resource-allocation problem. Evaluators vary in reliability, latency, and token cost, so one fixed evaluator may be an inefficient choice across tasks of different difficulty. R²Eval treats automated assessment as a combination of routing and aggregation, selecting evaluators for individual instances under explicit accuracy, latency, and cost constraints.

The study constructs six datasets with human reference assessments, covering mathematics, logic, code, knowledge, roleplay, and writing. It also examines how evaluator reasoning traces relate to assessment outcomes. The analysis finds substantial variation and systematic mismatches across difficulty levels, providing evidence that evaluator behavior depends on the difficulty regime.

The authors develop both offline and online strategies for allocating evaluation queries. Across 19 language models, these strategies improve the accuracy–efficiency trade-off relative to static baselines, reducing cost and latency while maintaining close agreement with human assessments. The findings support adapting evaluation resources to the instance, with routing forming a substantive part of assessment quality and efficiency.
icml-2026-routing-and-reasoned-evaluatio.tldr: R²Eval routes assessment queries by difficulty to reduce evaluation cost and latency while retaining close agreement with human judgments.
